original_question: Could individuals with macrosomia, macroglossia, or hemihyperplasia also present with Wilms tumor?

final_qi.question: Do individuals with macrosomia present with Wilms tumor?
final_qi.long_answer: Although isolated fetal or neonatal macrosomia does not itself cause a kidney tumour, one of the classic paediatric over-growth syndromes – Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (BWS) – is characterised by generalized macrosomia (large birth weight/size), organomegaly and hemihypertrophy. Children with BWS have a markedly increased risk of embryonal tumours, the most frequent of which is Wilms tumour (nephroblastoma). Because macrosomia is one of the cardinal clinical features of BWS, many infants and young children who manifest macrosomia in that context may later present with, or be screened for, Wilms tumour. Consequently, within accepted medical teaching, ‘macrosomia’ (as part of BWS or other over-growth conditions) is listed among the associations/predisposing features of Wilms tumour. Therefore, the statement that individuals with macrosomia can present with Wilms tumour is considered correct.

final_qi.question: Do individuals with macroglossia present with Wilms tumor?
final_qi.long_answer: Macroglossia is one of the hallmark clinical features of Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (BWS). Children with BWS have a markedly increased risk (roughly 5–10 %) of developing embryonal tumors, most commonly Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma). Consequently, when macroglossia is seen in the context of BWS or a similar overgrowth syndrome, clinicians perform periodic abdominal ultrasonography specifically to detect Wilms tumor at an early stage. Although macroglossia by itself does not cause Wilms tumor, its presence within the Beckwith-Wiedemann clinical picture is strongly associated with this renal malignancy, so the statement that individuals with macroglossia present with Wilms tumor is consistent with established medical consensus.

final_qi.question: Do individuals with hemihyperplasia present with Wilms tumor?
final_qi.long_answer: Isolated hemihyperplasia (formerly called hemihypertrophy) is a congenital over-growth disorder that carries a well-documented, significantly increased risk for embryonal tumors, especially Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma). Multiple large cohort and registry studies show a Wilms-tumor incidence of roughly 3–6 % in children with hemihyperplasia, markedly higher than the general population. Because of this recognized association, consensus surveillance guidelines recommend serial abdominal ultrasonography for Wilms tumor in all children with hemihyperplasia until at least 7 years of age. Therefore, while not every individual with hemihyperplasia will develop Wilms tumor, the condition is clinically linked to and may present with Wilms tumor, supporting the answer "yes."
